newsitem.title: USA: CME cattle seen unfazed by USDA, to follow cash.
newsitem.headline: CME cattle seen unfazed by USDA, to follow cash.

text.p: Chicago Mercantile Exchange cattle futures were expected to follow the lead set by cash cattle markets early next week as Friday's government Cattle on Feed Report was considered neutral to futures.
"This report doesn't give us any guidance," said Julia Bussie, analyst for AG Edwards.

She referred to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's news that the number of cattle on feed in the seven major states as of April 1 were up seven percent from a year ago, about equal to the average of analysts' estimates at 107.6 percent.
March placements came in at 102 percent of a year ago, near the average estimate of 103.3 percent and March marketings were 101 percent of a year earlier versus 100.6 percent estimated.
"It's (futures) going to be driven by what we sell (cash) cattle at next week and the beef" trend," said Karl Skold, Director of Research for Frontier Risk Management.
But Skold noted the USDA revised February placements up by 25,000 head which some traders might see as slightly bearish.
"It (placements) would imply a little bit more cattle that still need to be moved to market," he said.

Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp, noted that although placements at 102 percent were about as expected, they were still above a year ago and nine percent over the average of the last five years. It was also the largest placement figure since the 1,000-head-or-more feedlot capacity data figures were started in 1992.
He added that the on-feed number at 107 percent was 14 percent larger than the average for the last five years.
However, the report could also be viewed as slightly bullish for June and August based on marketings and the amount of slaughter cattle coming in during March from Canada.

"It appears that, because we may have imported less Canadian cattle for slaughter during the month of March, our steers and heifers represented a little larger total from the total slaughter mix and therefore we got a little bigger (marketing) figure than you could have expected," Levitt said
The marketing figure was three percent above the five-year average and "that means we are current on marketings coming into April," he said.

Levitt also noted that when the April live cattle futures contract goes off the board on Wednesday next week, June will have a $5 per hundredweight (cwt) discount to the cash market. June will look too cheap relative to cash and this may lift the June live cattle futures contract.
CME live cattle futures for June delivery on Friday closed at 64.475 cents a lb versus the top price paid in most of this week's cash cattle sales at $69.00 per cwt.
"The cash market probably will not be coming down quite as drastically between April and August as we might have anticipated (seasonally), but we are still going to have a break," Levitt added.
